Amolo
am'ə-lō
n. (Amolo, archbishop of Lyon 841–852, successor of Agobard, who wrote to Gottschalk during the predestination quarrel)
Frankish personal name, a diminutive of the root amal, labour, vigour.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Amolo followed Agobard as archbishop of Lyon in 841 and held the see through the first years of the Carolingian predestination quarrel. When Gottschalk of Orbais was condemned in 849, Hincmar of Reims sent his own account of the case to Lyon, and Amolo answered with a letter addressed to Gottschalk himself. The letter is a careful document. Amolo affirmed what Augustine taught, that God chose His elect by free grace before the world and that none of them perishes, and he rebuked several of Gottschalk's sharper propositions — among them that the baptized who afterward fall away were never truly washed, and that God takes no pleasure in any outward good of the reprobate. He urged the imprisoned monk to submit and to stop writing. What Amolo did not do was endorse Hincmar's universal articles; the church of Lyon under his successors became the chief defender of the doctrine Hincmar was trying to bury. Amolo's instinct was Paul's, that “The Lord knoweth them that are his” (2Ti 2:19), and that the same seal reads, “Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity” (2Ti 2:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines election in theology as the choice of persons to eternal life, and reprobation as the state of being abandoned to destruction.

expand to see more

ELEC'TION, n. In theology, divine choice; predetermination of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy, become subjects of grace, are sanctified and prepared for heaven.

REPROBA'TION, n. The act of abandoning, or state of being abandoned to eternal destruction.

EPIS'TLE, n. A writing directed or sent, communicating intelligence to a distant person; a letter.

Key Scripture

2Ti 2:19 — "Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity."

Eph 1:4 — "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:"

John 6:44 — "No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day."

Rom 8:30 — "Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified."

Modern Corruption

A pastoral middle voice in the Gottschalk affair — sound on election, too ready to counsel silence.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation Amolo represents is older and quieter: to agree with a persecuted man's doctrine in substance while advising him to stop confessing it. Eph 1:4 says God “hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4), and Amolo did not deny it. But a truth that may be held and not spoken has already been handed to the men who wish it unspoken.

The principle to recover is that doctrinal precision and pastoral counsel are not rivals. Amolo was right to correct Gottschalk where he overreached, and right that the golden chain of Rom 8:30 runs from predestination to glory without a broken link: “whom he did predestinate, them he also called” (Rom 8:30). He would have served the church better by saying as plainly to Reims what he said to the prisoner.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ginosko (G1097), to know; eklegomai (G1586), to choose; helko (G1670), to draw.

Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know; 2 Timothy 2:19.

Greek sphragis (G4973) — a seal; 2 Timothy 2:19.

Greek eklegomai (G1586) — to choose out; Ephesians 1:4.

Usage

"“The Lord knoweth them that are his” (2Ti 2:19) — the seal on the foundation."

"“No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (John 6:44) — the necessity of grace."

"“them he also glorified” (Rom 8:30) — the end of the chain."
